extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, scientists interested in methodology and reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the correctness, scope, and application of inductive and deductive reasoning in scientific argumentation, including when idealizations are permitted and how separate inductions may be combined to yield demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning is from particulars to particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The real inference is always from particulars to particulars: from the observed instances to an unobserved one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General propositions are mere formulæ adopted for guidance; the true premises are the individual observations even if forgotten or known only via others. Evaluate arguments by tracing whether particular observations legitimately warrant the particular conclusion claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: General propositions are guiding formulæ, not intermediate premises
rubrics_metrics.description: The successive general propositions are not steps in the reasoning, are not intermediate links in the chain of inference, between the particulars observed and those to which we apply the observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an argument, distinguish the actual observed instances (the real premises) from the general formulas used to apply those observations to new cases; check whether the formula accurately records the distinguishing marks that justify the induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine distinguishing marks for applying an induction
rubrics_metrics.description: We determine once for all what are the distinguishing marks by which such cases may be recognized, so that we may never fail to draw the induction when correctly applicable and avoid drawing it when not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically inspect the listed 'marks' or criteria that the author claims identify the class of cases to which an induction applies; ask whether those marks are sufficient and necessary and whether they are reliably observable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of marks-of-marks (indirect recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: We may recognize marks either at once, or by the aid of other marks, which by another induction we collected to be marks of the first; even these marks of marks may be recognized through a third set, producing a train of reasoning of any length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate chains that rely on inferred secondary or tertiary markers: each step must be supported by a prior legitimate induction. Identify and test each intermediate induction rather than accepting the terminal claim alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple inductive chains to reach complex conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductions often consist of several chains united at the extremity (e.g., 'a a mark of d, b of e, c of f, d e f of n, therefore a b c a mark of n').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the argument correctly brings together distinct inductions: verify each chain's validity and that their convergence legitimately yields the claimed conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring new cases within established inductions by inventive combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific ingenuity lies in so combining various inductions, as, by means of one within which the case evidently falls, to bring it within others in which it cannot be directly seen to be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an argument purports to extend a generalization to a new kind of case, require a clear showing of how existing inductions are composed to cover the new case and whether the selection of intermediate marks is plausible rather than ad hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer constructing sciences from fewest and simplest inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are weighty reasons for giving every science as much of the character of a Deductive Science as possible; for endeavoring to construct the science from the fewest and the simplest possible inductions, and to make these suffice by combination to prove complex truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging methodological quality, favor theories that reduce many phenomena to a small set of well-supported generalizations. Penalize unnecessary proliferation of independent generalizations without connecting principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: deductive vs experimental (not deductive vs inductive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The opposition is not between the terms Deductive and Inductive, but between Deductive and Experimental. A science is experimental in proportion as new cases require new observations (fresh inductions); deductive in proportion as conclusions about new cases can be drawn by bringing them under old inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify a body of work by whether it mainly requires fresh observation for each new problem or whether it successfully applies existing generalizations; evaluate claims accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic test for a science becoming deductive: availability of marks of marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference consists in our having been able, or not yet able, to discover marks of marks. If we can trace chains a→b→c→... so as to connect a to e, the science may be made deductive; otherwise it remains experimental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess efforts to render a field deductive by examining whether robust intermediate relations (marks of marks) have been established and tested, rather than assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: New inductions can transform experimental sciences into deductive ones
rubrics_metrics.description: A new set of instances, and a consequent new induction, may at any time bridge over the interval between unconnected generalizations, enabling deductive proofs that were not previously possible (Newton's unifying discovery is the prime example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of paradigm-shifting unification by asking if they demonstrably connect previously isolated regularities and whether the connecting induction is empirically robust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics (science of number) is a chief agent for deductivization
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of number applies to all things in respect of quantity; when variations of quality correspond to variations of quantity, mathematical formulas become marks of general truths and render the theory deductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating mathematical models applied to qualitative phenomena, verify the empirical basis for mapping quality to quantity and test whether the mathematical relations legitimately serve as intermediate 'marks'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map qualities to quantities with care (coordinate/algebraical transformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If varieties of qualities correspond regularly to varieties in quantities (or coordinates), algebraical treatment can make geometric or physical questions solvable by mathematics (Descartes/Clairaut example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand explicit justification for the correspondence between qualitative properties and quantitative variables and for the stability of that mapping across cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealizations in definitions are methodological conveniences, not literal truths
rubrics_metrics.description: The definitions of geometry (points, lines, circles) do not exactly correspond to real objects; they are convenient feignings to confine attention to properties material to the inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When authors use idealized definitions, check whether the idealization is explicitly acknowledged and whether corrections are introduced when idealization would produce appreciable error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical necessity is conditional on hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity ascribed to mathematical truths consists in their correctly following from the suppositions from which they are deduced; those suppositions are hypotheses and not strictly true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'necessary' or 'certain' conclusions as conditional: evaluate the truth and applicability of the underlying hypotheses before accepting claimed necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate conceiving ideal objects with having exact mental copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Points and lines as conceived are copies or abstractions from experience (minimum visible, lines with breadth); purely ideal mathematical objects do not exist in mind or nature exactly as defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims that rely on a priori conceivability; probe whether the supposed mental clarity is instead a methodological assumption required to make reasoning tractable.

rubrics_metrics.name: When idealization errors matter, add corrective propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: When extending inductions to cases in which the error from idealization would be appreciable, we correct conclusions by combining fresh propositions relating to the aberration or to material properties (e.g., expansion by heat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that extrapolations from idealized models include error analyses or corrective terms whenever physical irregularities might affect the outcome materially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrations should, when possible, be traced back to original inductive foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: To trace deductive truths to their inductive foundation, avoid proving from prior deductions alone; instead use the premises of earlier propositions (first principles) where available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In peer review, prefer reconstructions that exhibit how a deduction rests on primary inductive or empirical premises rather than circular reliance on previous theorems without grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms and simple formulas encapture the marks used throughout a deductive science
rubrics_metrics.description: All the inductions involved in a deductive science are comprised in a few simple formulæ (the Axioms and Definitions); the rest of the science consists of processes to bring unforeseen cases within those inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the adequacy of proposed axioms/definitions to serve as comprehensive marks for the phenomena claimed to follow from them; test whether many results truly reduce to those axioms or rest on additional, unstated premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess transformations from experimental to deductive by empirical breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformations depend on discovering that varieties of a phenomenon uniformly accompany varieties of some other, better-known phenomenon (e.g., sound ↔ oscillatory motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims of deducibility, ask for systematic empirical evidence showing the uniform correspondence across the range of cases, not just isolated examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware overclaiming universality from narrow generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: A science composed of detached and mutually independent generalizations (e.g., 'acids redden blues', 'alkalies make them green') remains experimental unless connections are shown; unconnected propositions cannot yield wide deductive reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine whether the work demonstrates genuine connections between separate generalizations or illegitimately extrapolates from isolated regularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of deductive conclusions limited by the certainty of their inductive bases
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusions of all deductive sciences must stand to the inductions or assumptions on which the science is founded; those inductions may be doubtful yet are treated as certain for the purposes of the science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In review, demand explicit statement of the inductive bases and assess their empirical support; downgrade claims of certainty when the underlying inductions are weak or contestable.
